items.title: dluxtras
items.text:
Extensions for ∂Lux: reusable pieces shared by several dLux-based projects.

AI disclosure

Most of the code in this repository, and its documentation, was either written or rewritten with Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant), under the direction and review of the repository owner. Treat it with the usual scrutiny, and check results that matter.

items.title: What's in it
items.text: Module Contents Guide dluxtras.spectra CombinedSpectrum / CombinedBasisSpectrum (a source spectrum times a system throughput), propagate_spectrum with Hermite wavelength sparsity, and recommend_wavelength_sampling. Spectra, sources and throughput dluxtras.sources HermitePointSource (honours Hermite sparsity) and PointSourceArcsec (position in arcsec, flux in detected photons). Spectra, sources and throughput dluxtras.throughput Loading and binning system throughput; spectrum_args builds a CombinedBasisSpectrum. Spectra, sources and throughput dluxtras.spectral_eigenmodes Spectral Fisher matrix, its eigenmodes, and the number of constrainable modes K, optionally marginalising any model parameter. Spectral eigenmodes dluxtras.spectral_bins optimal_bins: top-hat bins that best match the constrainable spectral modes, for reporting a recovered spectrum with its covariance. Spectral eigenmodes dluxtras.wavefront_eigenmodes MaskedPixelOPD (one OPD value per pupil pixel) and matrix-free wavefront Fisher eigenmodes, marginalising positions, pixel scale, focus or any other parameter. Wavefront eigenmodes dluxtras.eigenmodes The shared core: Fisher operators, marginalisation and leading_modes. Wavefront eigenmodes dluxtras.fitting FitProblem, Curvature and FisherFit: Fisher-whitened fitting with SGD, Nesterov momentum, L-BFGS or natural gradient, plus uncertainties. Fitting dluxtras.curvature Unit-free (Jacobi-normalised) Hessians, covariances and correlations. Unit-free Hessians

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "dluxtras @ git+https://github.com/milolangker/dluxtras.git"
# or, for development
git clone https://github.com/milolangker/dluxtras.git && pip install -e "./dluxtras[test]"

It needs dLux 0.15.x. Enable double precision before building models; the Fisher and fitting tools require it:

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

items.title: Quick example
items.text:
Build a broadband point source whose 100-bin spectrum is propagated at only 12 wavelengths, then fit its position:

import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

import numpy as np
import dLux as dl
from dluxtras import CombinedBasisSpectrum, FitProblem, PointSourceArcsec, gaussian_nll, spectrum_args

wavelengths = np.linspace(500e-9, 700e-9, 201)  # m
throughput = np.exp(-0.5 * ((wavelengths - 600e-9) / 40e-9) ** 2)
spectrum = CombinedBasisSpectrum(**spectrum_args(wavelengths, throughput, nwavels=100,
                                                 photons=1e6, n_coarse=12))

optics = dl.AngularOpticalSystem(256, 0.1, [dl.CircularAperture(0.05, normalise=True)], 64, 0.1, 2)
telescope = dl.Telescope(optics, PointSourceArcsec(spectrum=spectrum, position=np.zeros(2)))
data = telescope.set("source.position", np.array([0.02, -0.01])).model()

problem = FitProblem(telescope, {"source.position": np.zeros(2)}, data, gaussian_nll,
                     np.sqrt(data + 1.0))
fit = problem.fit(optimiser="lbfgs").run(50)
print(fit.params["source.position"], problem.curvature(fit.params, precondition="full").std)

items.title: Unit-free Hessians
items.text:
A Hessian in physical units has entries ∂²L/∂xᵢ∂xⱼ, so each row and column carries its parameter's units. Put a Zernike coefficient in metres (with a nanometre-scale effect) next to a flux of 1e6, and the diagonal spans ~30 decades. The matrix's condition number then reflects your choice of units, not anything physical.

dluxtras.curvature holds the Hessian in unit-free form:

\[ H = \frac{N}{s\,s^\top}, \qquad s_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|H_{ii}|}} \]

N (normalised) is dimensionless with a unit diagonal, and s carries the units. For a Fisher matrix, s_i is the conditional 1σ uncertainty of parameter i, with all others fixed. This is diagonal (Jacobi) scaling, also called equilibration. It's what LAPACK's xPOEQU does, and the same step as going from a covariance to a correlation matrix.

from dluxtras.curvature import scaled_hessian, scaled_covariance, correlation

normalised, s, unflatten = scaled_hessian(loss, params)   # params: a pytree, e.g. a dict
cov = scaled_covariance(normalised, s)                     # Cholesky on normalised, then rescale
sigma = unflatten(np.sqrt(np.diag(cov)))                   # back in your parameter structure
corr = correlation(normalised)                             # the scales cancel

For fitting, FitProblem.curvature computes the Fisher matrix directly in this form; see Fitting.

items.title: What units do and don't affect
items.text:
Measured on a dLux model: 8 Zernike coefficients in metres, position in radians, flux 1e8.

diag(H) range 1.9e-12 to 2.2e18 cond(H), raw 5.3e18 cond(normalised) 2.0

Comparing float32 against float64:

float32 computation error Hessian entries, raw units 1.3e-5 Hessian entries, rescaled before differentiating 1.3e-5 (identical) Marginal σ via inv(H) (LU) on the raw matrix 6e-6 Marginal σ via pinv(H) or eigh(H) on the raw matrix 100% wrong, in float64 too Marginal σ via scaled_covariance 6e-6
  • The Hessian itself is not unit-sensitive. Floating point has relative precision, and autodiff applies the chain rule exactly. Rescaling a parameter just rescales its row and column, so rescaling before differentiating gains nothing, except protection from float over/underflow (float32 covers roughly 1e±38).
  • Linear algebra that adds to or thresholds the matrix is unit-sensitive. That covers pinv, eigh, SVD and rcond cutoffs (all relative to the largest entry), damping or ridge terms (+ μI), and step-size normalisation. In raw units these silently discard the small-scale parameters; here they did so even in float64, since 5e18 exceeds float64's ~1e16 range of precision. Do them on normalised.
  • Real degeneracy survives normalisation. Correlations near ±1 between parameters are physical. cond(normalised) measures them, and no diagonal rescaling can do much better (within a factor of n; van der Sluis, 1969). In float32 you lose about log10(cond(normalised)) of the ~7 available digits, on top of the model's own float32 precision.

items.title: Float32 or float64?
items.text:
Normalisation removes the units reason to need float64. Three reasons can remain:

  1. Degeneracy. The error in the uncertainties is roughly (relative precision of the Hessian entries) × cond(normalised). With float32 models giving ~1e-5 entries, cond 1e3 already means ~1% errors.
  2. Large values with small uncertainties. If σ/|x| < ~1e-7, float32 cannot represent the parameter's value precisely enough, and no rescaling fixes that.
  3. Loss differences. A float32 negative log likelihood summed over a large image cannot resolve changes below ~0.1, while line searches and convergence tests need much smaller differences. This is why dluxtras.fitting requires jax_enable_x64.

items.title: Fitting
items.text:
dluxtras.fitting fits dLux (or any Zodiax) models by optimising in coordinates whitened by the Fisher matrix. This removes the problem of parameters with wildly different units, such as Zernike coefficients in metres next to a flux of 1e6. It also gives you uncertainties from the same machinery.

Three objects do the work:

  • FitProblem: what is fitted, i.e. the model, the parameters, the data and the likelihood.
  • Curvature: the Fisher matrix at one point, held in unit-free form. It provides the whitening and the uncertainties.
  • FisherFit: a resumable optimisation that records its history.

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)  # required

from dluxtras import FitProblem, gaussian_nll

params = {"source.position": np.zeros(2), "aberrations.coefficients": np.zeros(8)}
problem = FitProblem(telescope, params, data, gaussian_nll, std)

fit = problem.fit().run(200)                     # default
fit = problem.fit(optimiser="lbfgs").run(100)    # usually fastest; stops when converged
fit = problem.fit(precondition="full").run(10)   # natural gradient, near the minimum

sigma = problem.curvature(fit.params, precondition="full").std   # marginal 1-sigma
best = fit.fitted_model

items.title: Choosing a method
items.text:
Call Per step Use when 1 problem.fit() 1 gradient Default. Diagonal Fisher whitening and SGD with Nesterov momentum (lr 1, 0.9). Strictly first-order; the curvature is computed once. Robust from any start in the basin. 2 problem.fit(optimiser="lbfgs") ~1 gradient Usually fastest. Converged from every benchmark start, and stops on its own once converged. Add precondition="full" when you have up to a few hundred parameters. 3 problem.fit(precondition="full") 1 gradient Already near the minimum (a re-fit, a refined model). A natural-gradient (Newton) step; converges in 1–3 steps there. Unreliable from far away.

The benchmarks have the numbers behind these recommendations. In short:

  • L-BFGS needed the fewest gradients per fit almost everywhere.
  • The default is several times slower when parameters are strongly correlated, but never failed.
  • Natural gradient is unbeatable near the minimum and fails from far away.

Which preconditioner?

precondition="diagonal" (the default) only needs the diagonal of the Fisher matrix, so it scales to many parameters (e.g. pixel OPD maps). precondition="full" needs the whole matrix, which costs about n gradient evaluations and n² memory, and it also captures correlations. Below a few hundred parameters the full matrix is usually affordable, and in the benchmarks it was even cheaper to compute than the diagonal.

items.title: The likelihood
items.text:
FitProblem(model, params, data, nll, *nll_args) takes any negative log likelihood with the signature nll(prediction, data, *nll_args, **nll_kwargs) -> scalar. By default the prediction is model.set(params).model(); pass predict=lambda params, model: ... for anything else, e.g. several exposures stacked into one array.

  • Sum, don't average. Use a proper negative log likelihood, summed over pixels. The Fisher matrix, the uncertainties and the convergence test are all in its units, and a mean over pixels would make the uncertainties too large by √(number of pixels).
  • Mask NaN pixels before arithmetic. NaN in data marks excluded pixels. np.nansum gives NaN gradients at those pixels (JAX computes 0 × NaN = NaN), so mask with np.where first. The built-in gaussian_nll(prediction, data, std) does this.
  • Any likelihood works. Correlated noise (e.g. a row-correlated Gaussian) and Poisson noise are both fine. The Fisher matrix is computed from the likelihood you supply.
def poisson_nll(prediction, data):
    ok = ~np.isnan(data)
    return np.sum(np.where(ok, prediction - np.where(ok, data, 0.0) * np.log(prediction), 0.0))

problem = FitProblem(telescope, params, data, poisson_nll)

items.title: Choosing what to fit
items.text:
params is a dictionary of {path: array}. trainable selects entries. True/False fits or freezes a whole key, and a boolean array selects individual entries. Keys you don't mention are fitted. Frozen entries keep their starting values exactly.

problem = FitProblem(telescope, params, data, gaussian_nll, std,
                     trainable={"aberrations.coefficients": np.arange(8) < 4})  # first 4 only
problem.active_labels   # ['aberrations.coefficients[0]', ..., 'source.position[1]']

items.title: Running and resuming
items.text:
run(n) takes up to n steps and returns the fit, so calls chain. Everything is recorded before each step:

fit = problem.fit()
fit.run(200).run(200)        # resumes; optimiser state is kept
fit.losses                   # loss before each step
fit.active_history           # (n_steps, n_active), columns named by fit.active_labels
fit.param_history            # {key: (n_steps, *shape)}
fit.moves                    # step sizes, in conditional sigma
plt.plot(fit.active_history, label=fit.active_labels)

fit.refresh() recomputes the curvature where the fit is now, with the same settings, and restarts the optimiser from there. History is kept. It helps when the starting point was far off and the curvature has changed, e.g. problem.fit(precondition="full").run(5).refresh().

items.title: Stopping on convergence
items.text:
run stops early once two consecutive steps each move every parameter by less than tol conditional sigma. It then sets fit.converged = True.

  • Default: tol = 0.01 for optimiser="lbfgs", and off otherwise. In the benchmarks, L-BFGS stopped within 0.01σ of the minimum from every start, a few steps after the loss had converged.
  • Normalisation: because the test is in sigma, it doesn't depend on the absolute value of the loss. It only assumes the loss is a proper negative log likelihood.
  • Other optimisers: you can set tol for them too, e.g. problem.fit(precondition="full", tol=0.01). Small steps reliably mean convergence for L-BFGS and natural gradient, whose steps approach the full remaining distance. Diagonal SGD on correlated parameters can take small steps while still far away, so use a smaller tol there.
  • Turning it off: tol=0 never stops early. Avoid running L-BFGS far past convergence regardless: at the exact minimum its line search struggles, and steps cost about 10× more.

items.title: Uncertainties
items.text:
Compute the full curvature at the best fit:

c = problem.curvature(fit.params, precondition="full")
c.std               # marginal 1-sigma, in your dict shapes (frozen entries = 0)
c.covariance        # (n, n), ordered by c.labels
c.correlation       # (n, n) correlation matrix
c.conditional_std   # 1/sqrt(F_ii): 1-sigma with everything else fixed (optimistic)
c.condition_number  # degeneracy after removing units; large = near-degenerate parameters
  • Default kind: kind="expected" (the default) is the Fisher matrix. That gives the Cramér–Rao bound, and it's exact for fixed-(co)variance Gaussian and for Poisson noise.
  • Observed information: kind="observed" uses the actual Hessian of the loss against the data, an accepted alternative at the best fit.
  • Frozen parameters are treated as known, not marginalised over.

items.title: Curvature
items.text:
problem.curvature(params=None, *, precondition, kind, damping, curvature_data, batch_size):

Option Values Meaning precondition "diagonal" (default), "full" Compute the diagonal only (enough to whiten; no covariances), or the whole matrix. kind "expected" (default), "observed" The Fisher matrix, computed with the data replaced by the model prediction (always positive semi-definite), or the actual Hessian of the loss (can be indefinite away from the minimum; always computes the full matrix). damping float ≥ 0, "full" only Adds damping × each diagonal entry before whitening, for near-singular problems. Covariances stay undamped. curvature_data array, "observed" only Data to differentiate against instead of the problem's data. batch_size int How many derivative columns at once; memory only.

items.title: Optimiser
items.text:
problem.fit(curvature=None, optimiser=None, tol=None, **curvature_options):

  • None (default) picks the right SGD for the preconditioner: Nesterov momentum for diagonal, plain natural gradient for full. Momentum is not used with full whitening, where the curvature is already the identity: it only adds overshoot, and it failed from far starts in the benchmarks.
  • "lbfgs" is optax.lbfgs(), with a line search, so there's no learning rate. It reuses the line search's value and gradient, so a step costs about one gradient.
  • Any optax transform works and receives gradients in whitened coordinates. For example, optax.sgd(1.0) gives plain SGD, and optax.sgd(0.7, 0.9, nesterov=True) is the default with a wider stability margin, if a default fit oscillates. Avoid optax.adam: its per-parameter rescaling undoes the whitening, and it never converged from far starts in the benchmarks.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
The fit optimises u, where the active parameters are x = x0 + T u. T is chosen so that the curvature in u at the start point x0 is (close to) the identity. All linear algebra uses the unit-free normalised Fisher matrix F_n = S F S, with S = diag(1/sqrt(diag F)); see unit-free Hessians.

  • Diagonal: T = S / sqrt(λ_max(F_n)). λ_max is estimated by power iteration (about 20 Fisher-vector products), so a step with lr 1 is a Newton step along the stiffest direction, and plain gradient descent is stable for lr < 2. Correlated directions converge at about λ_min/λ_max per step, which momentum largely fixes. Nesterov momentum 0.9 at lr 1 is stable while the whitened curvature stays below ~1.36.
  • Full: T = S L⁻ᵀ, where L Lᵀ = F_n + damping·I. Gradient descent in u is then natural-gradient descent with the Fisher matrix frozen at x0: lr 1 is a Newton (Fisher-scoring) step.
  • Expected Fisher: F = Jᵀ H J, where J is the Jacobian of the prediction and H the Hessian of the likelihood with respect to the prediction. It's evaluated with the data replaced by the prediction, so it's exact for any likelihood whose score vanishes there (fixed-covariance Gaussian, Poisson) and always positive semi-definite.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Problem Fix ValueError: No positive curvature (freeze these parameters) Those parameters don't affect the prediction at this point. Freeze them with trainable, or move the start (e.g. even Zernikes at exactly zero aberration have no first-order effect). ValueError: Normalised curvature is singular or indefinite (full) Some combination of parameters is (nearly) degenerate. Freeze one of them, use the diagonal preconditioner, or set damping=0.01. ValueError: Nonfinite curvature Usually NaN gradients from NaN pixels: mask with np.where in your nll. FloatingPointError: Nonfinite loss/gradient The step diverged and no update was applied. Lower the learning rate, use L-BFGS, or refresh(). The default fit oscillates Pass optimiser=optax.sgd(0.7, 0.9, nesterov=True), or use L-BFGS. A fit is slow Use L-BFGS, or precondition="full" if n is modest. Check problem.curvature(..., precondition="full").condition_number: large values mean genuinely correlated parameters. It converges to the wrong answer No method here escapes a wrong local minimum. Use several starts, fit coarse-to-fine (low-order terms first), or enumerate known ambiguities (e.g. the even-Zernike sign flip).

items.title: Performance notes
items.text:
• Steps cost about one gradient. That's true of every method here, including L-BFGS, whose line search usually accepts its first trial step. The model evaluation dominates; the optimiser's own work is negligible.
  • A compiled loop barely helps. Running the whole solve inside one compiled JAX loop (as optimistix does) saved only 2–9% over the Python loop here; see the benchmarks. The Python loop keeps history, progress bars and resumable run(n).
  • Whitening matters more than the library. Run on raw dLux parameters, optimistix's BFGS failed to converge. In the whitened coordinates, it matched this module's L-BFGS. To use another optimiser library, minimise lambda u: problem.loss(c.active + c.transform @ u) with c = problem.curvature(...).
  • Float64 is required (jax_enable_x64). The whitening itself would work in float32, but line searches and convergence tests need loss differences that float32 can't resolve for large images.

items.title: Fitting benchmark: which FisherFit method to use
items.text:
Reproduce with:

python benchmarks/fitting_benchmark.py          # ~10 min
python benchmarks/fitting_benchmark.py --quick  # ~1 min, one start per distance
python benchmarks/loop_speed.py                 # compiled loops and optimistix (optional)
python benchmarks/optimistix_bfgs.py           # optimistix BFGS inside FisherFit (optional)

Run on 2026-10-16, Apple M5 Pro CPU, jax 0.11.2, dLux 0.15.1, optax 0.2.8, optimistix 0.1.0.

items.title: The three main options
items.text:
Call Per step Use when 1 problem.fit() 1 gradient Default. Diagonal Fisher whitening + SGD with Nesterov momentum (lr 1, 0.9). Strictly first-order, curvature computed once. 2 problem.fit(optimiser="lbfgs"), or with precondition="full" ~1 gradient Fewest gradients per fit almost everywhere, converged from every start, and stops on its own. Use "full" when n is modest (up to a few hundred). 3 problem.fit(precondition="full") 1 gradient Natural gradient (plain SGD, lr 1). Already near the minimum: 1–3 steps. Unreliable from far away.

Whichever you use, get uncertainties from problem.curvature(fit.params, precondition="full").std.

items.title: Recommendations
items.text:
1. The default (Nesterov, diagonal) converged from every start. It took 7–67 steps for the uncorrelated problem (n = 11) and 19–107 for the correlated one (n = 33), versus 6–86 and 106–944 for plain SGD at lr 1. Nesterov at lr 1 is only stable while the whitened curvature stays below ~1.36 (plain SGD: 2). It never failed here, but if a fit oscillates, use optax.sgd(0.7, 0.9, nesterov=True), which costs ~10–20% more steps.
  2. L-BFGS costs about one gradient per step: its line search usually accepts the first trial point, and the next step reuses that value and gradient. It needed the fewest gradients per fit in almost every case (table below), and converged from all 24 starts with either preconditioner. It stops on its own once converged (below); avoid forcing it far past convergence (tol=0), since at the exact minimum its line search struggles and steps cost ~10× more.
  3. Natural gradient (full whitening, plain SGD lr 1) converged in 1–3 steps from 3σ and 30σ. From 300σ it converged on only 2/3 starts (n = 11) and 0/3 (n = 33). Refreshing the curvature after 5 steps helped from the physical start (32 → 9 and 54 → 11 steps) but not reliably from 300σ.
  4. Don't add momentum to full whitening. The whitened curvature is already ~identity, so momentum has nothing to accelerate and only overshoots: Nesterov with "full" failed from the physical start at both sizes. That's why the default optimiser depends on the preconditioner.
  5. Avoid Adam. Its per-parameter rescaling undoes the Fisher whitening; it never converged from 300σ or the physical start. Plain (heavy-ball) momentum 0.9 overshoots on easy problems (39 steps vs Nesterov's 7 at 3σ, n = 11).
  6. Old spectrum default (diag(F⁻¹) preconditioning normalised by λ_max, lr 0.5) was the slowest method everywhere: 13–2371 steps.

items.text:
FisherFit.run stops once two consecutive steps each move every parameter by less than tol conditional sigma; L-BFGS uses tol = 0.01 by default. For each tolerance below, the cells show steps until the stop / steps until the loss was within 0.01 of the minimum / final error in marginal sigma. Each is the worst case over the starts at that distance.

Looser tolerances save a few steps but can stop early: with diagonal whitening on the correlated problem, tol = 0.1 stopped up to 0.3σ short, because L-BFGS had not yet learned the correlated directions and was still taking small steps along them.

items.title: Cost of the curvature
items.text:
At these sizes the full Fisher was cheaper to compute than the diagonal: 0.11 s vs 0.15 s at n = 11, and 0.13 s vs 0.18 s at n = 33. The diagonal's 20 power iterations, used to estimate λ_max, cost more than the extra columns of the full matrix. Both timings include JIT compilation, which dominates for a model this cheap.

For a slow, real model where compilation is negligible, rough costs are: - Diagonal Fisher: about n forward-mode passes plus about 60 gradients for the power iteration. - Full Fisher: about 2–3 gradients per parameter.

So the diagonal only becomes cheaper beyond a few tens to ~100 parameters, and fits that use it need more steps. In total cost the full Fisher stays ahead until n reaches the hundreds, which is also roughly where the n × n matrix and its O(n³) Cholesky start to matter.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
• Model: a 64-pixel pupil with Zernike aberrations (in metres), plus source position (radians) and flux. Point source, 3 wavelengths, ~1e6 detected photons, Gaussian noise with variance data + 10. Parameter units span about 15 decades.
  • Data: noiseless, so the truth is the exact minimum.
  • Problem sizes: n = 11 (8 Zernikes, cond(F_n) ≈ 3) and n = 33 (30 Zernikes, strongly correlated, cond(F_n) ≈ 94).
  • Starts: k marginal σ from the truth along random correlated directions (3 draws each, loss excess ≈ k²/2). Plus one "physical" start: 10 nm rms coefficient errors, a 40 mas position offset and a 30% flux error.
  • Converged means the loss is within 0.01 of the minimum, statistically negligible (≲ 0.15σ in the worst direction). Each run stops once converged.
  • Cells show median steps (starts converged / starts) / wall time. Wall time = curvature setup + steps × time per step. Every step is timed along the real trajectories; the column shows the method's median, excluding the first step (which includes compilation). Caps: 3000 SGD steps, 300 L-BFGS steps.
  • One gradient (value_and_grad) took about 1.1 ms. SGD and L-BFGS steps each cost about one gradient.

items.title: n = 11 parameters (8 Zernikes + position + flux), cond(F_n) at truth = 2.95
n = 33 parameters (30 Zernikes + position + flux), cond(F_n) at truth = 94

items.title: Compiled loops and optimistix
items.text: Does compiling the whole solve into one JAX loop, as optimistix.minimise does, make fits faster? benchmarks/loop_speed.py fits the n = 33 problem from the physical start, on the cheap model and on a ~13× heavier one. All rows except the last minimise the same Fisher-whitened loss; the last hands optimistix the raw parameters.

  • Compiling the loop saves 2–9%. That's the same L-BFGS steps run from Python vs inside one lax.fori_loop, i.e. the Python dispatch overhead per step. The model evaluation dominates, increasingly so for heavier models.
  • optimistix's BFGS is competitive in whitened coordinates: ~15–45% faster at a loose tolerance (rtol=atol=1e-4, comparable final error), similar at a tight one. Its backtracking line search and dense BFGS update are as efficient as optax's L-BFGS here.
  • On raw parameters it failed: 2000+ steps, still 300σ from the minimum. BFGS starts from an identity curvature, which in raw units treats a 1e-9 m coefficient and a 1e6 flux as the same size. The whitening matters, not the library. To use optimistix with whitening, minimise lambda u: problem.loss(c.active + c.transform @ u) with c = problem.curvature(...).

Without the compiled loop, the speed advantage measured above disappears. Driving optimistix step by step also relies on its solvers' init/step methods and on closure conversion, and its LBFGS cannot be carried between calls this way. So FisherFit keeps optax's L-BFGS. optimistix remains a good choice for a one-shot compiled solve in the whitened coordinates.

items.title: Caveats
items.text:
• The model is a cheap toy (1 ms per gradient), so the absolute times are dominated by JIT compilation. Compare methods by step counts, and by setup cost in gradients, when extrapolating to your own models.
  • Real data is harder. Noise, model mismatch and multiple minima (e.g. the sign ambiguity of the even Zernikes) make things harder than this noiseless single-source case.
  • Low signal changes the picture. At very low signal the Fisher can change several-fold within a few σ. In one 187-photon test, both diagonal and full plain SGD failed while L-BFGS converged from a far start; its near-start run was never completed. That is another reason to prefer L-BFGS's line search when unsure.
  • Small scale. Only 3 random starts per distance and n ≤ 33. Rerun the script after changes, or adapt make_problem to resemble your own data.
  • Local minima are not tested. All starts here sit in the truth's basin. None of these methods reliably escapes a wrong basin, momentum included: there's no gradient noise in full-image fits. Use multiple starts, coarse-to-fine fitting, or explicit enumeration of known ambiguities instead.

items.title: Spectra, sources and throughput
items.text: These modules describe a broadband source as seen through an instrument: a source spectrum, times the system throughput, propagated through dLux optics. They can propagate far fewer wavelengths than the spectrum has bins, using Hermite wavelength sparsity.

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
• Wavelengths are in metres everywhere. load_throughput reads other units and converts.
  • Throughput is dimensionless and excludes the source spectrum: optics × filter × detector QE, as appropriate for your bench.
  • Incident vs detected photons. spec_weights() is the incident photons per bin (before throughput), and filt_weights the mean throughput per bin. So:
    • spectrum.flux = incident photons = sum(spec_weights())
    • spectrum.proper_flux() = detected photons = sum(spec_weights() * filt_weights)
  • spectrum_args(..., photons=) sets the incident count, split evenly over the bins.
  • Positions: PointSourceArcsec takes arcsec. A plain dl.PointSource, and HermitePointSource, take radians.

items.title: Building a spectrum
items.text:
spectrum_args turns sampled wavelengths and throughput into the arguments of a CombinedBasisSpectrum. It bins the throughput into nwavels bins of mean throughput, trims the band where throughput is below threshold (default 1%) of its peak, and by default gives every bin an independent photon count (an identity basis):

from dluxtras import CombinedBasisSpectrum, spectrum_args, load_throughput

table = load_throughput("bench_throughput.dat", wavelength_unit="um")  # (n, 2): [m, throughput]
args = spectrum_args(table[:, 0], table[:, 1], nwavels=100, photons=1e6)
spectrum = CombinedBasisSpectrum(**args)
spectrum.proper_flux()   # detected photons

Pass basis and basis_weights to describe the spectrum with fewer coefficients, e.g. the spectral eigenmodes from Spectral eigenmodes. proj applies a further linear map to the coefficients. Use CombinedSpectrum directly for a subclass with its own spec_weights().

Other throughput helpers:

  • bin_throughput returns bin centres and mean throughput.
  • fractional_bandwidth returns Δλ/λ_c and the central wavelength.
  • filter_integrate and trim_throughput are the building blocks of the above.

items.title: Sources
items.text:
Use the sources in dluxtras.sources rather than dl.PointSource with these spectra:

  • HermitePointSource behaves like dl.PointSource, but honours the spectrum's n_coarse and low_memory. With neither set, it's identical to dl.PointSource.
  • PointSourceArcsec additionally takes its position in arcsec, and sets its flux to the spectrum's detected flux, spectrum.proper_flux(). So the image sums to about the detected photon count, minus light falling outside the stamp.
import dLux as dl
from dluxtras import PointSourceArcsec

telescope = dl.Telescope(optics, PointSourceArcsec(spectrum=spectrum, position=np.zeros(2)))
image = telescope.model()

items.title: Hermite wavelength sparsity
items.text:
A broadband PSF is a weighted sum of monochromatic PSFs, one per wavelength bin. Within a band the PSF varies smoothly with wavelength, so it's enough to propagate a few coarse nodes, each with its derivative with respect to wavelength (one forward-mode pass gives both), and cubic-Hermite-interpolate the rest.

spectrum = CombinedBasisSpectrum(**spectrum_args(wl, tp, nwavels=100, photons=1e6, n_coarse=12))
spectrum.coarse_wavelengths   # the 12 wavelengths actually propagated
  • n_coarse=None (the default) propagates every wavelength.
  • An integer propagates that many evenly spread nodes, both ends included.
  • low_memory=True propagates nodes one at a time, recomputing them in the backward pass. Peak memory is about that of one node, and gradients are ~1.5–2× slower. It works with or without n_coarse.

items.title: How many wavelengths?
items.text:
recommend_wavelength_sampling(K, photons) gives a recommendation from the number of constrainable spectral modes K (see Spectral eigenmodes) and the detected photon count N. Its empirical rules come from a point source with Poisson noise, requiring the model error to stay below Δχ² < 1, tested across 4 filters, 32–256 px stamps and N = 1e8–1e10. Neither rule ever undershot, there or in a generic re-check.

  • Hermite: n_coarse = max(3, 2K), with n_fine = max(300, 20K) fine wavelengths. Fine wavelengths are almost free with Hermite.
  • Exact: n_exact = ceil(23.5 K^0.553 (N/1e9)^0.208).

One Hermite node costs about jvp_cost (default 2.5) exact wavelengths. If the estimated speedup n_exact / (jvp_cost · n_coarse) is below min_speedup (default 1.5), it recommends plain propagation of n_exact wavelengths instead.

from dluxtras import recommend_wavelength_sampling

rec = recommend_wavelength_sampling(K=6, photons=1e9)
rec["n_coarse"], rec["n_fine"], rec["sparse"], rec["speedup"]

items.title: Low-level pieces
items.text: propagate_spectrum(optics, spectrum, offset, flux) is what the sources call. It's equivalent to optics.propagate(spectrum.wavelengths, offset, spectrum.weights * flux), but honours n_coarse and low_memory. coarse_indices and hermite_node_coeffs give the node positions and the Hermite interpolation weights.

items.title: Spectral eigenmodes
items.text: How many independent numbers about a source's spectrum can an image actually measure? The spectral Fisher matrix answers this. Its eigenvectors are the spectral shapes the data constrain, ordered from best to worst, and K, the number of constrainable modes, sets how finely you need to sample wavelengths (see Spectra).

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

from dluxtras.throughput import spectrum_args
from dluxtras.spectral_eigenmodes import spectral_eigenmodes, constrainable_modes, mode_criterion

args = spectrum_args(wavelengths_m, throughput, nwavels=100, photons=1e9)
modes = spectral_eigenmodes(telescope, args, k=100, noise="poisson")
K = constrainable_modes(modes)       # modes with 1 / (|a0| sqrt(d_i)) < 0.1
criterion = mode_criterion(modes)    # the value for every mode

telescope can be a dl.Telescope, bare optics (a telescope is created; optionally pass detector=), or a list of models sharing the spectrum, e.g. several dithers.

items.title: What is computed
items.text:
• Coordinates. The Fisher matrix is over incident photons per wavelength bin (before throughput). Every other parameter is held fixed unless you marginalise it.
  • Construction. It's Σ Jᵀ diag(1/variance) J, built from first derivatives only (no Hessian), with one monochromatic response computed at a time.
  • Noise model. noise="poisson" uses the reference image as the variance, which needs predictions in counts. noise="gaussian" takes a fixed variance (a scalar or an image-shaped array; a variance, not a standard deviation). variance_fn=lambda mu: ... overrides both, e.g. mu + read_noise**2.
  • Excluded pixels. bad_masks= excludes pixels. Pass one mask for every model, or a list with one mask (or None) per model; variance works the same way.
  • Detector. It's differentiated at the full polychromatic reference, so a differentiable nonlinear detector is handled locally.

spectral_eigenmodes does it all in one call. The steps are available separately: attach_spectrum (put a SpectralSource on the model), spectral_fisher (the matrix), and leading_modes (its k largest eigenpairs, as unit-norm columns).

The result, SpectralModes, holds: - values: the eigenvalues d_i. - vectors: unit-norm columns. - residuals: eigen-residuals (~1e-15 here; the matrix is dense). - sigma: 1σ per mode. - coefficients(bin_flux): projects a spectrum onto the modes, e.g. to use as basis_weights.

These fields match WavefrontModes from wavefront eigenmodes, and the two modules take the same keyword arguments.

items.title: Marginalising nuisance parameters
items.text:
By default the position, pixel scale, wavefront and so on are treated as perfectly known. In a real fit some of them are fitted too, which costs spectral information. List them to marginalise them, i.e. to compute the information left once they are fitted freely:

modes = spectral_eigenmodes(optics, args, k=100,
                            marginalise=["source.position"],
                            marginalise_shared=["optics.psf_pixel_scale"])
  • marginalise=[...] nuisances are per model: each model gets its own copy (e.g. each dither's position).
  • marginalise_shared=[...] nuisances are one copy shared by all models (e.g. the pixel scale).
  • Each entry is a model key, or an array of directions in bin-flux space. For example, the reference spectrum itself as a direction marginalises the overall flux scale.

This is exact (a Schur complement of the joint Fisher matrix), works with mixed units, and uses the same machinery as wavefront eigenmodes.

items.title: Example: does an unknown pixel scale matter?
items.text:
PSF size scales with λ / pixel scale, so an unknown pixel scale should be partly degenerate with the spectrum's colour. Here's a 1 m circular aperture, 48 × 48 px at 0.06″/px (Nyquist at 600 nm), 100 bins and 1e10 incident photons, with a ~20% band (550–650 nm):

marginalised K criterion, modes 1–6 nothing 11 1.1e-5, 8.3e-5, 1.7e-4, 2.6e-4, 3.8e-4, 6.5e-4 source position 11 identical to 3 digits pixel scale 11 1.1e-5, 1.6e-4, 1.8e-4, 3.8e-4, 4.2e-4, 1.1e-3 position + pixel scale 10 1.1e-5, 1.6e-4, 1.8e-4, 3.8e-4, 4.4e-4, 1.2e-3

A ~40% band (480–720 nm) behaved the same way, with K going from 21 to 20.

  • The pixel scale mainly costs the second mode, the spectral slope or colour. Its uncertainty roughly doubles, and later modes lose 7–70%.
  • The first mode is unaffected. That's the total flux.
  • Position marginalisation costs nothing: a shift is orthogonal to a colour change.
  • K drops by at most one, because one marginalised parameter removes roughly one direction's worth of information. So marginalise the pixel scale whenever it is fitted or uncertain; it matters most for the low-order colour terms.

items.title: The constrainable-mode criterion
items.text:
Mode i is constrainable if its fractional uncertainty is below 10%:

\[ \frac{1}{|a_0|\sqrt{d_i}} < 0.1 \]
  • d_i is the Fisher eigenvalue.
  • a_0 = v_0 · q_0 is the reference spectrum's coefficient on the leading mode.

K is the number of modes that pass; constrainable_modes(modes, threshold=0.1).

  • Compute all modes. Use k equal to the number of wavelength bins. If every computed mode passes, K is only a lower bound and a warning is issued.
  • Sample finely enough. Use ≳ 100 bins for wide bands; K is not converged at ~30 bins.
  • Use the real flux. The criterion scales as N^(-1/2) with the detected photon count N (the reference image sum), so build the Fisher matrix at the real flux. Null modes (d_i = 0) give infinity.
  • Mind the metric. The eigenvectors are unit-norm in incident-photons-per-bin coordinates, a metric that depends on the wavelength sampling; no bin-width whitening is applied.

Then use K to choose wavelength sampling: recommend_wavelength_sampling(K, photons=N) suggests n_coarse ≈ 2K.

items.title: Reporting the spectrum in bins
items.text:
After fitting the spectrum in the eigenmode basis, only the first K modes are measured; the rest stay at the reference spectrum. To report the result as K top-hat bins, choose bins that the measured modes can fully represent. Otherwise the unmeasured modes leak into the bin values as bias.

optimal_bins places the edges. With B the bin matrix (row k is the fraction of each fine wavelength cell inside bin k) and P = V Vᵀ the projector onto the K modes, the leakage of bin k is the fraction of the bin outside the modes' span:

\[ L_k = \frac{\lVert B_k (I - P)\rVert^2}{\lVert B_k\rVert^2} \]

The edges minimise the mean leakage, and every mode counts equally. Since top-hats don't overlap, K bins for K modes give the same optimum whether you ask how well the modes represent the bins or how well the bins represent the modes.

from dluxtras import optimal_bins, constrainable_modes

K = constrainable_modes(modes)
V = modes.vectors[:, :K]
bins = optimal_bins(V, modes.wavelengths)                     # free widths
bins = optimal_bins(V, modes.wavelengths, equal_widths=True)  # only the outer edges move

# After fitting coefficients c in that basis, with covariance C (e.g. diag(1 / values)):
flux, cov = bins.bin_modes(c, C, reference=modes.reference)                # photons per bin
density, dcov = bins.bin_modes(c, C, reference=modes.reference, density=True)  # per metre
bins.edges, bins.centres, bins.widths, bins.leakage
  • Outer edges may move inward by up to max_edge_shift (default 10% of the span), to trim poorly constrained band tails. max_edge_shift=0 fixes them.
  • Free widths are always at least one fine cell wide.
  • The search is global. The objective has kinks wherever an edge crosses a fine cell boundary, so the outer edges are first scanned on a grid, then polished. The free-width search starts from that equal-width optimum, so free widths are never worse than equal widths.
  • Your own modes work too. modes can be a SpectralModes, or any orthonormal columns with their wavelengths, e.g. eigenvectors of the observed information at your best fit.

items.title: Equal widths vs free widths, and the choice of normalisation
items.text:
Here are both options for the 8 leading F606W modes (101 cells, 4700–7200 Å):

bins outer edges mean leakage equal widths (equal_widths=True) 4749.8–7117.1 Å 0.162 free widths optimised 0.144 (bins 253–338 Å wide)

With equal widths, the mean leakage is the same quantity as the width-weighted Σ‖B_k(I−P)‖² / Σ‖B_k‖²; on these modes the two agreed to 0.35% or better (cells cut by an edge are the only difference). Optimising either one finds the same outer edges, to within 0.3 Å.

With free widths they differ, and the width-weighted form fails. It lets the optimiser shrink seven bins to zero width and give the eighth the whole band (a "leakage" of 0.002), which is why each bin is normalised separately here.

items.title: Wavefront eigenmodes
items.text:
Which wavefront shapes can an image actually measure, and how well? The Fisher matrix of a wavefront parameterisation answers this. Its leading eigenvectors are the OPD shapes the data constrain best, and 1/sqrt(eigenvalue) is each shape's 1σ uncertainty.

dluxtras.wavefront_eigenmodes computes these matrix-free: the Fisher matrix is only ever applied to vectors, and its leading eigenpairs come from Lanczos iteration. That makes one free OPD value per pupil pixel (thousands of parameters) practical. Nuisance parameters (source positions, pixel scale, focus terms, anything in the model) can be marginalised.

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
import jax
jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

from dluxtras.wavefront_eigenmodes import MaskedPixelOPD, nuisance_shapes, wavefront_eigenmodes

fit_opd = MaskedPixelOPD(pupil)   # pupil: the aperture's transmission array
models = [m.set("optics", m.optics.insert_layer(("fit_opd", fit_opd), 1)) for m in models]

modes = wavefront_eigenmodes(models, "optics.fit_opd.coefficients", k=6,
                             variance_fn=lambda mu: mu + read_noise**2)
modes.values      # eigenvalues, descending
modes.sigma       # 1-sigma of each mode's coefficient, in nm
modes.maps()      # (6, ny, nx) mode maps, NaN outside the pupil
modes.residuals   # Lanczos residuals; check they are small

items.title: The pixel OPD layer
items.text:
MaskedPixelOPD(transmission, threshold=0) adds one OPD coefficient, in nm, per transmitting pupil pixel.

  • It only adds OPD. Transmission stays with the aperture layer, so insert it in the same pupil plane, on the same grid (index 1, right after the aperture, in the example).
  • Pick a fresh layer name, e.g. "fit_opd", if the optics already contain an OPD layer.
  • threshold excludes faint edge pixels from the fit, but not from the optics.
  • Static OPD can stay. Any existing static OPD stays in the optical train, so the modes are computed about that reference.

The key doesn't have to be a pixel OPD, though. wavefront_eigenmodes(models, key) works for any parameter vector of the model, e.g. "optics.aberrations.coefficients" of a Zernike BasisOptic.

items.title: Several exposures
items.text:
Pass a list of models (e.g. dithers, rolls, defocused images). They share one wavefront: the parameter at key is set to the same q0 in every model (by default, its value in the first). Each model's own flux must already include its integration time. A single model with a stacked (n_exposures, ny, nx) output also works.

Noise options are the same as for spectral eigenmodes:

  • noise="poisson" (the default) uses the reference image as the variance, so it must be in counts.
  • noise="gaussian" takes a fixed variance.
  • variance_fn=lambda mu: ... overrides both.
  • bad_masks excludes pixels.
  • Per model, or for all: variance and bad_masks can be a list with one entry per model, or a single value used for all of them.

items.title: Marginalising nuisance parameters
items.text:
By default every other model parameter is held fixed at its reference value. That's optimistic when, in a real fit, you'd also fit the source positions or a focus term: the wavefront then has to share information with them. Listing them marginalises them, i.e. computes the information about the wavefront left once those nuisances are fitted freely.

There are two lists:

  • marginalise=[...] nuisances are per model: each exposure gets its own independent copy. Use it for things that change between exposures, such as source positions.
  • marginalise_shared=[...] nuisances are shared: one copy for all models. Use it for properties of the instrument, such as the pixel scale.

Each entry is either a model key or an array of directions in the parameter's space. Mix them freely:

modes = wavefront_eigenmodes(
    models, "optics.fit_opd.coefficients", k=10,
    marginalise=["source.position", nuisance_shapes(fit_opd, ["defocus"])],
    marginalise_shared=["optics.psf_pixel_scale"],
)
  • A key (e.g. "source.position", "source.flux", "optics.psf_pixel_scale", or a BasisOptic's coefficients) marginalises every entry of that parameter.
  • Directions marginalise those shapes' coefficients. nuisance_shapes(layer, terms) gives orthonormal tip, tilt and defocus shapes over a MaskedPixelOPD's pixels, plus any custom shapes you pass. The resulting modes are then orthogonal to them.

All nuisances are marginalised together, exactly, via the Schur complement of the joint Fisher matrix:

\[ F_\mathrm{marg} = F_{qq} - F_{q\eta}\,F_{\eta\eta}^{+}\,F_{\eta q} \]
  • Mixed units are safe. F_ηη is pseudo-inverted in unit-free (Jacobi-normalised) form, so radians, arcseconds and photons can be mixed.
  • Invisible nuisances are ignored. Combinations the data can't see at all are dropped rather than causing an error.
  • Cost. Each nuisance costs one extra derivative evaluation per model, done once when the operator is built.

Tip/tilt: OPD shapes or source position?

A tip/tilt OPD and a source offset move the image the same way, so marginalising either removes (almost) the same information. Marginalising both at once is harmless: the pseudo-inverse handles the degeneracy.

items.title: Piston and other null modes
items.text:
OPD piston doesn't change images, so for MaskedPixelOPD keys it is projected out by default (remove_piston=True). Other null directions remain possible:

  • Relative pistons between disconnected pupil segments.
  • Directions at a symmetric, aberration-free reference that have zero first-order effect but second-order effects.

Request only as many modes as are informative, and check values.

items.title: Units and normalisation
items.text: vectors[:, i] has unit Euclidean norm over the active pixels. A modal coefficient c (nm) is the OPD c * vectors[:, i], whose pupil RMS is |c| / sqrt(N_active). For unit-RMS maps, multiply maps() by sqrt(N_active) and divide sigma by it. Eigenvalues depend on this convention and on the pupil sampling.

items.title: Lower-level pieces
items.text:
• wavefront_fisher(models, key, ...) returns a FisherOperator. F(v) gives F @ v, and F.dense() builds the matrix for small problems.
  • leading_modes(F, k, project_out=...) (in dluxtras.eigenmodes) diagonalises either a dense matrix or an operator.
  • mode_maps(layer, vectors) scatters vectors onto the pupil grid.

items.title: Validation: how many wavelengths?
items.text:
recommend_wavelength_sampling(K, N) (see Spectra) turns the number of constrainable spectral modes K and the detected photon count N into a number of wavelengths to propagate:

  • Hermite: n_coarse = max(3, 2K) coarse nodes on a fixed fine grid;
  • Exact: n_exact = ceil(23.5 K^0.553 (N/1e9)^0.208) wavelength bins.

Both rules were fitted to JWST/NIRCam models. This page re-derives them on generic optics and synthetic filters, using only dluxtras, dLux, JAX and NumPy, and checks whether either rule ever asks for too few wavelengths.

Reproduce with:

python validation/wavelength_sampling.py          # ~6 min
python validation/wavelength_sampling.py --quick  # ~30 s, 1 pupil, 2 filters, 2 stamps

Run on 2026-10-16, Apple M5 Pro CPU, jax 0.11.2, dLux 0.15.1, NumPy 2.5.4 (full run: 375 s).

items.title: Setup
items.text:
• Optics. dl.AngularOpticalSystem, D = 1 m, 256-pixel pupil, oversample 3, summed to detector pixels. Two pupils:
    • clear: an unobscured, unaberrated circle;
    • obscured: a 20% central obscuration, four spider vanes 1% of D wide, and 50 nm RMS of random Zernike aberration (Noll 4–11, about λ_c/20, Strehl ~0.9).

  • Filters. Four synthetic smooth top-hats centred on 1 µm, with tanh edges and a 20% linear throughput tilt (like a QE slope). Their fractional bandwidths (at 1% of peak, as fractional_bandwidth measures them) and λ_c/D in detector pixels match the four NIRCam filters of the original study:

    filter Δλ/λ_c λ_c/D [px] mimics N3 0.030 2.14 F212N M17 0.166 1.86 F182M W29 0.291 2.20 F444W W53 0.530 1.62 F322W2

  • Stamps of 32, 64, 128 and 256 px, i.e. half-widths R_half of 7–80 λ_c/D. The source sits at a sub-pixel offset of (0.3, −0.2) px with a flat incident spectrum.

  • Photons N = 1e8, 1e9 and 1e10, where N is the detected photon count in the stamp (the truth image sum).

items.title: Method
items.text:
For each (pupil, filter, stamp):

  1. Truth. 600 exact monochromatic PSFs on the spectrum_args(nwavels=600) grid, summed with CombinedBasisSpectrum.weights.
  2. K. The Fisher matrix in incident-photons-per-bin coordinates, with Poisson variance equal to the image, is built once at unit flux from the cached PSFs. K(N) then follows analytically, since the criterion 1/(|a0| sqrt(d_i)) scales as N^-1/2; it's counted with constrainable_modes (threshold 0.1).
  3. Model error. Δχ² = N Σ_p (I_model − I_truth)² / I_truth, with both images divided by the truth sum.
  4. Minimum n_coarse. Hermite images on the same 600-bin spectrum, so only the interpolation error enters. Every integer n_coarse from 3 upwards is scanned, and the minimum is the smallest value beyond which every scanned value has Δχ² < 1. (Δχ²(n_coarse) isn't monotonic: node alignment makes it ripple, in 18 of 32 cases.)
  5. Minimum n_exact. Exact images from spectrum_args(nwavels=n) with their own binning, so this is the quadrature error. Found on a grid, then bisected to the integer.
  6. Rules. Both rules are evaluated at K(N) with recommend_wavelength_sampling. Each prediction's own image is then tested: a rule undershoots if Δχ² ≥ 1 there.

The script also runs these consistency checks:

  • the truth equals dl.Telescope(optics, HermitePointSource(...), detector).model() to 1e-14;
  • the cached Hermite images match HermitePointSource(n_coarse=...) (Δχ² to 1e-11);
  • the Fisher matrix equals spectral_eigenmodes to 4e-15, with the same K at the library's photon count;
  • 600 vs 900 bins in the hardest case (W53, 256 px) gives Δχ² ≤ 1.2e-3 at N = 1e10.

items.title: Conclusion
items.text:
Neither rule undershot in any of the 96 cases (Δχ² < 1 at the prediction in 96/96 for both). The generic setup reproduces the NIRCam study closely: K is typically 5–20% above the NIRCam values for the matching filter and stamp (by 0–1 for the narrowest filter), and min n_coarse / K spans 0.75–1.50 (NIRCam: 0.87–1.78). Both rules are confirmed, and both are conservative:

  • Hermite, max(3, 2K): at least 1.33× the minimum (median 1.9×). The tightest cases are at N = 1e10. max(3, ceil(1.45 K)) would already have sufficed here (NIRCam needed 1.70), so c = 2 leaves about 20–40% headroom for setups less benign than these.
  • Exact, 23.5 K^0.553 (N/1e9)^0.208: at least 1.31× the minimum, but with a median of 2.3× and up to 4.7×. The overshoot grows with stamp size. At fixed filter and N, the minimum n_exact barely depends on the stamp (W29 at 1e10: 91–134 from 32 to 256 px), while K roughly triples, so the K^0.553 term over-predicts for large stamps.

Caveats:

  • The speedup estimate is biased towards Hermite. recommend_wavelength_sampling estimates the speedup as n_exact / (2.5 n_coarse) with the conservative n_exact rule. Against the measured minimum n_exact, it predicts ≥ 1.5× when the true figure is below 1.5× in 36 of 96 cases, mostly narrow filters or small K at high N (e.g. N3 at 32 px: estimated 1.8–4.1×, true 0.6–1.2×). The recommendation is still safe (both rules are), but it can pick the slower option. The jvp_cost of 2.5 was not re-measured here.
  • The filters are smooth. The quadrature error, and so n_exact, depends on how sharp the throughput is. Real filters with steeper edges or ripples need more bins. At N = 1e10, NIRCam's F322W2 needed 150–200 (on a coarse grid), against 103–145 for W53 here. Check n_exact with a real throughput curve before relying on a margin as small as 1.3×.
  • The tested range is narrow. These results cover one source position, a flat source spectrum, Poisson noise only, 600 fine bins, and N = 1e8–1e10, the range the rules were fitted on.

items.title: Curvature
items.text:
Unit-free (diagonally equilibrated) Hessians.

A Hessian in physical units has entries d2L / dx_i dx_j, so its rows and columns carry each parameter's units. A Zernike coefficient in metres with a nm-scale effect gives entries ~1e18 larger than a parameter of order one, and the matrix's condition number then reflects units rather than real degeneracy between parameters.

These functions hold the Hessian as

H = normalised / outer(s, s),    s = 1 / sqrt(|diag(H)|)

where normalised is dimensionless with a unit diagonal (Jacobi scaling) and s carries the units. For a Fisher matrix, s_i is the conditional 1-sigma of x_i (all other parameters fixed). Do linear algebra on normalised and reapply s at the end; never invert the physical-units matrix directly, and never apply damping, ridges or eigenvalue cutoffs to it.

Normalisation removes ill-conditioning caused by units only. Degeneracy between parameters (correlations near +-1) survives it: cond(normalised) measures that, and is within a factor n of the best any diagonal rescaling can achieve (van der Sluis, 1969). dluxtras.fitting builds on these functions.

def scaled_hessian(f, x, scales=None, *, nbatches=1, jit=True, checkpoint=False):
    """Hessian of a scalar function, returned in unit-free form.

    Differentiates `f(x0 + c * u)` at `u = 0` with `zodiax.diffops.hessian`, then
    normalises the result to a unit diagonal. Rescaling does not change the accuracy of
    the Hessian itself (floating point and autodiff are scale-invariant); `scales` only
    keeps intermediate values away from float over/underflow.

    Parameters
    ----------
    f : callable
        Scalar function of a pytree, e.g. a negative log likelihood.
    x : PyTree
        Point to evaluate at, e.g. `{"coefficients": ..., "position": ...}`.
    scales : None, float or PyTree, optional
        Rough characteristic size of each parameter in its own units: a scalar, or a
        pytree matching `x` whose leaves broadcast to `x`'s leaves, e.g.
        `{"coefficients": 1e-9, "position": 1e-7}`. Order-of-magnitude guesses are
        enough. Default `None` (all ones).
    nbatches : int, optional
        Passed to `zodiax.diffops.hessian` (memory). Default 1.
    jit : bool, optional
        Passed to `zodiax.diffops.hessian`. Default True.
    checkpoint : bool, optional
        Passed to `zodiax.diffops.hessian`. Default False.

    Returns
    -------
    normalised : Array
        `(n, n)` Hessian with unit diagonal: zero where a parameter has no curvature
        and -1 where its curvature is negative.
    s : Array
        `(n,)` scales in `x`'s units, with `H = normalised / outer(s, s)`.
    unflatten : callable
        Maps a flat `(n,)` vector back to `x`'s structure.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `scales` are not finite and positive.
    """
    x_flat, unflatten = ravel_pytree(x)
    c = _flat_scales(scales, x)
    if not bool(np.all(np.isfinite(c) & (c > 0))):
        raise ValueError("scales must be finite and positive")

    # Differentiate in u where x = x0 + c * u, evaluated at u = 0.
    H_u, _ = hessian(
        lambda u: f(unflatten(x_flat + c * u)),
        np.zeros_like(x_flat),
        nbatches=nbatches,
        jit=jit,
        checkpoint=checkpoint,
    )
    H_u = (H_u + H_u.T) / 2

    # Jacobi-normalise. Parameters with zero curvature keep their input scale.
    d = np.abs(np.diag(H_u))
    r = np.where(d > 0, 1 / np.sqrt(np.where(d > 0, d, 1)), 1)
    normalised = r[:, None] * H_u * r[None, :]
    return normalised, c * r, unflatten

def scaled_covariance(normalised, s):
    """Covariance `inv(H)` in the parameters' own units, via Cholesky of `normalised`.

    Requires `normalised` to be positive definite (e.g. a Fisher matrix, or the Hessian
    of a negative log likelihood at a minimum); otherwise the result is NaN.

    Parameters
    ----------
    normalised : Array
        `(n, n)` unit-free matrix.
    s : Array
        `(n,)` scales.

    Returns
    -------
    Array
        `(n, n)` covariance. Marginal uncertainties are `np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))`.
    """
    factor = jsl.cho_factor(normalised, lower=True)
    inverse = jsl.cho_solve(factor, np.eye(normalised.shape[0], dtype=normalised.dtype))
    inverse = (inverse + inverse.T) / 2
    return s[:, None] * inverse * s[None, :]

def correlation(normalised):
    """Correlation matrix of the covariance `inv(H)`, from `normalised` alone.

    The scales cancel, so `s` is not needed.

    Parameters
    ----------
    normalised : Array
        `(n, n)` unit-free, positive-definite matrix.

    Returns
    -------
    Array
        `(n, n)` correlation matrix with unit diagonal.
    """
    factor = jsl.cho_factor(normalised, lower=True)
    inverse = jsl.cho_solve(factor, np.eye(normalised.shape[0], dtype=normalised.dtype))
    d = 1 / np.sqrt(np.diag(inverse))
    return d[:, None] * inverse * d[None, :]

items.title: Eigenmode core
items.text:
Shared machinery for Fisher eigenmodes with marginalised nuisance parameters.

dluxtras.spectral_eigenmodes and dluxtras.wavefront_eigenmodes both compute the Fisher matrix of one parameter vector q of a model (bin fluxes, or per-pixel OPD), optionally marginalised over nuisance parameters, and its leading eigenmodes. This module holds the parts they share.

Nuisance parameters are given as a list whose entries can be mixed freely:

  • a model key (str), e.g. "source.position" or "optics.psf_pixel_scale": every entry of that parameter becomes a nuisance;
  • an array of directions in q-space, shape (len(q),) or (len(q), m), e.g. wavefront_eigenmodes.nuisance_shapes(layer) for tip, tilt and defocus: the coefficients of those directions become nuisances.

marginalise nuisances are per model: every model (e.g. every exposure) gets its own independent copy, as for per-exposure source positions. marginalise_shared nuisances are one set shared by all models, as for a common pixel scale. Both are marginalised together, exactly, via the Schur complement of the joint Fisher matrix:

F_marg = F_qq - F_qn F_nn^+ F_nq

i.e. the information about q left once all nuisances are fitted freely. F_nn is inverted in Jacobi-normalised (unit-free) form, so nuisances with very different units (radians, arcseconds, photons) can be mixed, and a pseudo-inverse drops nuisance combinations the data cannot see at all (e.g. OPD piston).

All Fisher matrices here are sum J.T W J with per-pixel weights W = 1 / variance frozen at the noiseless reference prediction (pixels uncorrelated). Enable jax_enable_x64 before building models.

def leading_modes(fisher, k=6, *, project_out=None, tol=1e-7, ncv=None, maxiter=None, seed=0):
    """The `k` largest eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a Fisher matrix.

    A dense matrix is diagonalised exactly (`eigh`); a `FisherOperator` (or any
    `matvec` with a `size`) uses restarted Lanczos (SciPy `eigsh`), which never forms
    the matrix.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fisher : Array or FisherOperator
        Symmetric positive semi-definite Fisher matrix, dense `(n, n)` or matrix-free.
    k : int, optional
        Number of modes. Default 6.
    project_out : Array, optional
        Directions `(n,)` or `(n, m)` to project out before diagonalising, e.g. a column
        of ones for OPD piston. The modes are then orthogonal to them. Default None.
    tol : float, optional
        Lanczos convergence tolerance (matrix-free only). Default 1e-7.
    ncv : int, optional
        Lanczos vectors (matrix-free only). Default `max(2k + 1, 20)`, capped at `n`.
    maxiter : int, optional
        Lanczos iterations (matrix-free only). Default SciPy's.
    seed : int, optional
        Seed of the Lanczos start vector (matrix-free only). Default 0.

    Returns
    -------
    Eigenpairs
        `(values, vectors, residuals)`. Dense eigenvalues below roundoff are set to 0.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `k` is out of range, the matrix is not square, or (dense) it has a
        significantly negative eigenvalue.
    FloatingPointError
        If a matrix-free product is not finite.
    """
    dense = not isinstance(fisher, FisherOperator) and not callable(fisher)
    if dense:
        fisher = onp.asarray(fisher, dtype=float)
        if fisher.ndim != 2 or fisher.shape[0] != fisher.shape[1]:
            raise ValueError("fisher must be square")
        n = fisher.shape[0]
    else:
        n = int(fisher.size)
    Q = None
    if project_out is not None:
        P = onp.asarray(project_out, dtype=float).reshape(n, -1)
        Q = onp.linalg.qr(P)[0]
    available = n - (0 if Q is None else Q.shape[1])
    if not isinstance(k, (int, onp.integer)) or not 1 <= k <= available - (0 if dense else 1):
        raise ValueError(f"Require 1 <= k <= {available - (0 if dense else 1)} for this matrix")

    def project(v):
        return v if Q is None else v - Q @ (Q.T @ v)

    if dense:
        F = (fisher + fisher.T) / 2
        if Q is not None:
            F = project(project(F).T).T
        values, vectors = onp.linalg.eigh(F)
        values, vectors = values[::-1], vectors[:, ::-1]
        scale = max(float(onp.max(onp.abs(values))), onp.finfo(float).tiny)
        if values[-1] < -1e-9 * scale:
            raise ValueError("Significantly negative Fisher eigenvalue")
        values = onp.where(values > 10 * n * onp.finfo(float).eps * scale, values, 0.0)
        values, vectors = values[:k], vectors[:, :k]

        def apply(v):
            return F @ v
    else:
        def apply(v):
            v = project(onp.asarray(v, dtype=float).reshape(n))
            result = onp.asarray(fisher(v), dtype=float).reshape(n)
            if not onp.isfinite(result).all():
                raise FloatingPointError("Non-finite Fisher-vector product")
            return project(result)

        operator = LinearOperator((n, n), matvec=apply, dtype=onp.float64)
        ncv = min(n, max(2 * k + 1, 20)) if ncv is None else ncv
        v0 = project(onp.random.default_rng(seed).normal(size=n))
        values, vectors = eigsh(operator, k=k, which="LA", v0=v0, tol=tol, ncv=ncv,
                                maxiter=maxiter)
        order = onp.argsort(values)[::-1]
        values, vectors = values[order], vectors[:, order]
    # Consistent display sign; eigenvector signs have no physical meaning.
    pivots = onp.argmax(onp.abs(vectors), axis=0)
    vectors = vectors * onp.where(vectors[pivots, onp.arange(k)] < 0, -1.0, 1.0)
    denominator = onp.maximum(onp.abs(values), onp.finfo(float).tiny)
    residuals = onp.array([onp.linalg.norm(apply(vectors[:, i]) - values[i] * vectors[:, i])
                           / denominator[i] for i in range(k)])
    return Eigenpairs(values, vectors, residuals)

def noise_weights(mu, *, noise="poisson", variance=1.0, variance_fn=None, bad_mask=None):
    """Per-pixel Fisher weights `1 / variance`, zero at excluded pixels.

    Parameters
    ----------
    mu : Array
        Noiseless reference prediction (any shape, e.g. an image or a stack).
    noise : {"poisson", "gaussian"}, optional
        `"poisson"` (default) uses `variance = mu`, so `mu` must be in counts and
        strictly positive on included pixels. `"gaussian"` uses `variance`.
    variance : float or Array, optional
        Gaussian variance (not standard deviation): a scalar or an array broadcastable to
        `mu`. Ignored for Poisson noise or when `variance_fn` is given. Default 1.
    variance_fn : callable, optional
        `variance_fn(mu) -> variance` overrides both noise choices, e.g.
        `lambda mu: mu + read_noise**2`. Evaluated once, at the reference.
    bad_mask : Array, optional
        Boolean, the shape of `mu`; True excludes a pixel.

    Returns
    -------
    Array
        Weights with the shape of `mu`.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `noise` is invalid, the mask does not match `mu` or excludes every pixel, the
        reference is not finite (or negative, for Poisson) on included pixels, or the
        included variances are not finite and positive.
    """
    if noise not in ("gaussian", "poisson"):
        raise ValueError("noise must be 'gaussian' or 'poisson'")
    mu = onp.asarray(mu, dtype=float)
    keep = onp.ones(mu.shape, dtype=bool) if bad_mask is None else ~onp.asarray(bad_mask, bool)
    if keep.shape != mu.shape or not keep.any():
        raise ValueError("Bad mask must match the model output and retain pixels")
    if not onp.isfinite(mu[keep]).all() or (noise == "poisson" and onp.any(mu[keep] < 0)):
        raise ValueError("Invalid reference prediction on included pixels")
    if variance_fn is not None:
        var = variance_fn(np.asarray(mu))
    else:
        var = mu if noise == "poisson" else variance
    var = onp.broadcast_to(onp.asarray(var, dtype=float), mu.shape)
    if not onp.all(onp.isfinite(var[keep]) & (var[keep] > 0)):
        raise ValueError("Included variances must be finite and positive; mask zero-mean "
                         "Poisson pixels explicitly")
    return np.asarray(onp.where(keep, 1 / onp.where(keep, var, 1.0), 0.0))

items.text:
Fisher-preconditioned fitting for dLux/Zodiax models.

A FitProblem holds what is fitted (model, parameters, data and likelihood). Its curvature method computes the Fisher matrix in unit-free form, and its fit method returns a resumable FisherFit that optimises in Fisher-whitened coordinates.

The three main ways to fit are:

problem = FitProblem(model, params, data, gaussian_nll, std, trainable=mask)
fit = problem.fit().run(200)                        # 1. diagonal Fisher, Nesterov SGD
fit = problem.fit(optimiser="lbfgs").run(100)       # 2. L-BFGS (stops when converged)
fit = problem.fit(precondition="full").run(10)      # 3. natural gradient
sigma = problem.curvature(fit.params, precondition="full").std   # marginal 1-sigma

Enable jax_enable_x64 before building models. See the "Fitting" guide in the documentation for when to use each option.

The Fisher matrix (or loss Hessian) at params, in unit-free form.

With kind="expected" this is the Fisher matrix F = J.T H J, where J is the Jacobian of the prediction and H the Hessian of nll with respect to the prediction, with the data replaced by the prediction (NaN pixels kept). That is exactly the Fisher matrix for Gaussian noise of fixed (co)variance, correlated or not, and for Poisson noise, and it is positive semi-definite everywhere.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default params dict

Where to evaluate it. Default is the problem's initial parameters. Frozen entries always take the problem's values.

None precondition (diagonal, full)

"diagonal" (default) computes only the diagonal of F, plus its largest normalised eigenvalue by power iteration; that is enough for whitening but not for covariances. "full" computes the whole matrix.

"diagonal" kind (expected, observed)

"expected" (default) is the Fisher matrix described above. "observed" is the Hessian of the loss against the actual data (or curvature_data), which includes residual terms and can be indefinite away from the best fit. "observed" always computes the full matrix.

"expected" damping float

Added to the normalised matrix's diagonal before whitening, so 0.01 adds 1% of each diagonal entry. Only for precondition="full", to whiten near- singular problems. Covariances stay undamped. Default 0.

0.0 curvature_data Array

Data to use instead of the problem's data. Only for kind="observed".

None batch_size int

How many derivative columns to compute at once. Affects memory only. Default 1.

1

Type Description Curvature

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a parameter has no positive curvature (freeze it), if the curvature is not finite, or if precondition="full" and the normalised matrix is singular or indefinite (freeze degenerate parameters or set damping).

def curvature(self, params=None, *, precondition="diagonal", kind="expected", damping=0.0,
              curvature_data=None, batch_size=1):
    """The Fisher matrix (or loss Hessian) at `params`, in unit-free form.

    With `kind="expected"` this is the Fisher matrix `F = J.T H J`, where `J` is
    the Jacobian of the prediction and `H` the Hessian of `nll` with respect to
    the prediction, with the data replaced by the prediction (NaN pixels kept).
    That is exactly the Fisher matrix for Gaussian noise of fixed (co)variance,
    correlated or not, and for Poisson noise, and it is positive semi-definite
    everywhere.

    Parameters
    ----------
    params : dict, optional
        Where to evaluate it. Default is the problem's initial parameters. Frozen
        entries always take the problem's values.
    precondition : {"diagonal", "full"}, optional
        `"diagonal"` (default) computes only the diagonal of `F`, plus its
        largest normalised eigenvalue by power iteration; that is enough for
        whitening but not for covariances. `"full"` computes the whole matrix.
    kind : {"expected", "observed"}, optional
        `"expected"` (default) is the Fisher matrix described above. `"observed"`
        is the Hessian of the loss against the actual data (or `curvature_data`),
        which includes residual terms and can be indefinite away from the best
        fit. `"observed"` always computes the full matrix.
    damping : float, optional
        Added to the normalised matrix's diagonal before whitening, so 0.01 adds
        1% of each diagonal entry. Only for `precondition="full"`, to whiten near-
        singular problems. Covariances stay undamped. Default 0.
    curvature_data : Array, optional
        Data to use instead of the problem's data. Only for `kind="observed"`.
    batch_size : int, optional
        How many derivative columns to compute at once. Affects memory only.
        Default 1.

    Returns
    -------
    Curvature

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If a parameter has no positive curvature (freeze it), if the curvature is
        not finite, or if `precondition="full"` and the normalised matrix is
        singular or indefinite (freeze degenerate parameters or set `damping`).
    """
    if precondition not in ("diagonal", "full"):
        raise ValueError("precondition must be 'diagonal' or 'full'")
    if kind not in ("expected", "observed"):
        raise ValueError("kind must be 'expected' or 'observed'")
    if not (onp.isfinite(damping) and damping >= 0):
        raise ValueError("damping must be finite and nonnegative")
    if damping and precondition == "diagonal":
        raise ValueError("damping only applies to precondition='full'")
    if curvature_data is not None and kind == "expected":
        raise ValueError("curvature_data only applies to kind='observed'")
    if int(batch_size) != batch_size or batch_size < 1:
        raise ValueError("batch_size must be a positive integer")

    x = self.selection.initial_active if params is None else self.selection.active_of(params)
    n = x.size
    if kind == "expected":
        mu, jvp = jax.linearize(self.predict, x)
        reference = np.where(np.isnan(self.data), np.nan, mu)
        nll_grad = jax.grad(lambda m: self.nll(m, reference))

        def hvp(t):  # Hessian of nll in prediction space, times t
            return jax.jvp(nll_grad, (mu,), (t,))[1]

        if precondition == "diagonal":
            def column_curvature(v):
                t = jvp(v)
                return np.sum(t * hvp(t))

            diagonal = _batched(column_curvature, n, batch_size, x.dtype)
            matrix = None
        else:
            pullback = jax.vjp(self.predict, x)[1]
            matrix = _batched(lambda v: pullback(hvp(jvp(v)))[0], n, batch_size, x.dtype)
    else:
        data = self.data if curvature_data is None else np.asarray(curvature_data)
        loss_grad = jax.grad(lambda a: self.loss(a, data))
        matrix = _batched(lambda v: jax.jvp(loss_grad, (x,), (v,))[1], n, batch_size,
                          x.dtype)
    if matrix is not None:
        matrix = (matrix + matrix.T) / 2
        diagonal = np.diag(matrix)
    if not bool(np.all(np.isfinite(diagonal))):
        raise ValueError("Nonfinite curvature: check that nll has finite gradients at "
                         "NaN pixels (see gaussian_nll)")
    bad = [label for label, d in zip(self.active_labels, onp.asarray(diagonal)) if not d > 0]
    if bad:
        raise ValueError(f"No positive curvature (freeze these parameters): {bad}")
    scales = 1 / np.sqrt(diagonal)

    normalised = eigenvalues = None
    if matrix is not None:
        normalised = scales[:, None] * matrix * scales[None, :]
        eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(normalised)
        lambda_max = float(eigenvalues[-1])
    else:
        pullback = jax.vjp(self.predict, x)[1]
        fvp = jax.jit(lambda v: scales * pullback(hvp(jvp(scales * v)))[0])
        lambda_max = _largest_eigenvalue(fvp, n)

    if precondition == "diagonal":
        transform = scales / np.sqrt(lambda_max)
    else:
        damped = normalised + damping * np.eye(n, dtype=x.dtype)
        values = np.linalg.eigvalsh(damped)
        if not float(values[0]) > 1e-12 * float(values[-1]):
            raise ValueError(
                f"Normalised curvature is singular or indefinite (eigenvalues "
                f"{float(values[0]):.3g} to {float(values[-1]):.3g}). Freeze degenerate "
                "parameters, use kind='expected', or set damping > 0."
            )
        inverse_factor = jsl.solve_triangular(
            np.linalg.cholesky(damped), np.eye(n, dtype=x.dtype), lower=True
        )
        transform = scales[:, None] * inverse_factor.T

    return Curvature(self.selection, x, kind, precondition, damping, curvature_data,
                     batch_size, scales, normalised, eigenvalues, lambda_max, transform)

def fit(self, curvature=None, optimiser=None, tol=None, **curvature_options):
    """Start a resumable `FisherFit` where the curvature was evaluated.

    Parameters
    ----------
    curvature : Curvature, optional
        The curvature to whiten with. Default computes one with
        `self.curvature(**curvature_options)`.
    optimiser : None, "lbfgs" or optax.GradientTransformation, optional
        `None` (default) picks SGD with lr 1: with Nesterov momentum 0.9 for a
        diagonal curvature, plain (natural gradient) for a full one. `"lbfgs"` is
        `optax.lbfgs()`. Any optax transform also works; it receives gradients
        in whitened coordinates. Avoid `optax.adam`, which undoes the whitening.
    tol : float, optional
        Stop once steps move every parameter by less than `tol` conditional sigma;
        see `FisherFit`. Default 0.01 for `"lbfgs"` and 0 (no early stop) otherwise.
    **curvature_options
        Passed to `curvature` when no `curvature` is given, e.g.
        `precondition="full"`.

    Returns
    -------
    FisherFit

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If both `curvature` and `curvature_options` are given.
    """
    if curvature is not None and curvature_options:
        raise ValueError("Pass either a Curvature or curvature options, not both")
    if curvature is None:
        curvature = self.curvature(**curvature_options)
    return FisherFit(self, curvature, optimiser, tol)

Because it is measured in sigma, the test does not depend on the likelihood's normalisation, provided nll is a proper (summed) negative log likelihood. Default 0.01 for "lbfgs" and 0 (no early stop) otherwise. Small steps reliably mean convergence for L-BFGS and natural gradient, whose steps approach the whole remaining distance. Diagonal SGD on correlated parameters can take small steps while still far away, so use a smaller tol there.

def __init__(self, problem, curvature, optimiser=None, tol=None):
    self.problem = problem
    if tol is None:
        tol = 0.01 if isinstance(optimiser, str) and optimiser == "lbfgs" else 0.0
    if not (onp.isfinite(tol) and tol >= 0):
        raise ValueError("tol must be finite and nonnegative")
    self.tol = float(tol)
    self.optimiser = _make_optimiser(optimiser, curvature.precondition)
    self.losses, self.history, self.moves, self.steps = [], [], [], 0
    loss = problem.loss
    optimiser = self.optimiser
    # Line-search optimisers (L-BFGS) store the value and gradient at the accepted
    # point; reusing them avoids recomputing both at the start of the next step.
    probe = optimiser.init(np.zeros_like(curvature.active))
    reuse = all(optax.tree_utils.tree_get(probe, name) is not None
                for name in ("value", "grad"))

    @jax.jit
    def step(u, state, center, transform, scales):
        def value(v):
            return loss(center + _apply(transform, v))

        if reuse:
            loss_value, grad = optax.value_and_grad_from_state(value)(u, state=state)
        else:
            loss_value, grad = jax.value_and_grad(value)(u)
        updates, state = optimiser.update(grad, state, u, value=loss_value, grad=grad,
                                          value_fn=value)
        new_u = optax.apply_updates(u, updates)
        finite_loss = np.isfinite(loss_value) & np.all(np.isfinite(grad))
        finite_step = np.all(np.isfinite(new_u))
        move = np.max(np.abs(_apply(transform, new_u - u)) / scales)
        return loss_value, new_u, state, finite_loss, finite_step, move

    self._step = step
    self._restart(curvature)
